b: The story “The Sleep Car” begins with sunrise. A train rolls through a small city, with the narrator “watching cars waiting at the crossing, catching a glimpse of people walking on the city streets with bags slung over the arms.” She remarks that “seeing people in this way, a single frame of their life while my own blazed past … reminded me that we are all our own main characters.” The narrator admires her “cozy,” “well-thought-out” room, considers writing a novel, and walks around the train, imagining the stories of strangers with a notebook in her pocket. She sees two men playing chess and a mother and daughter eating asparagus soup. Snow falls, and she gets “lost staring out at the mountains, a faint halo of moon behind the clouds.” The narrator returns to her room: “I set my notebook beside the bed,” she says in the final line, “thinking that I might dream up a whole new story overnight, and wake to find myself in a new world.”

I listened to this story in bed, and it bored me so much that I couldn’t make it to the end without falling asleep. On the second night, I managed to reach the description of the dinner on the train, but I passed out before the narrator looked upon the moon. Finally, on the third night, I made it to the end of the story—and found it started over again, a second time, but at a slower and even more sleep-inducing pace. And I was riveted.

What an experiment, what a thrill! A story written to be neither listened to nor cared about. The premise refutes everything I’ve learned as a writer; it breaks the sacred laws of prose. Adult sleep stories have become one of the most popular genres of writing over the past decade, with nearly half of all podcast listeners using podcasts to help them fall asleep and millions of people listening and subscribing to popular sleep podcasts like Calm, Nothing Much Happens, and Sleep with Me. Yet few writers have commented on them. Why?
Because they are just podcasts, because we fall asleep before we reach the end, because serious writers don’t consider them serious writing.

Yet, the sleep podcast, the grown-up bedtime story, offers something new: a specialized story that refutes the laws of good writing. Readers have infinite options for books that let them turn off their brain, but sleep podcasts are uniquely fascinating—and somehow experimental, radical—because they reject every principle of writing, including the all-important desire to have a reader care at all. They don’t want you to listen; they don’t want you to empathize with the characters; they don’t want you to get to the end of the story. Sleep stories are anti-literature. A successful sleep story is a story you forget. And in these stories, instead of narrative hooks and the dramatic arcs of rollercoasters, we find storytelling as a broom: a simple object from the back of the closet made to clear the debris of daily life.
On a carpet of simple words, we glide to the freedom of dreams.

This is how you write to make someone fall asleep. Narrate simple actions in the present. Avoid consonants, and “observe the beauty of nature in all its exquisite detail.” According to one article in the New York Times, the perfect adult bedtime story must be “engaging but not overstimulating,” the “characters can’t be too complex,” but the details must be “very descriptive,” and the narrator must speak with the right “cadence, tone and energy” to create “a perceived connection and an element of dependability.” The writing guide for Get Sleepy lays out additional fundamentals: plain diction, grateful characters, and little dialogue. Stories should also avoid “common fears/issues/insecurities like claustrophobia, arachnophobia, infertility, loss of grandparents, alcohol use, concerns about weight or appearance, etc.” A writer for Sleep with Me describes his stories as “bad first drafts,” rambling and tangential (it turns out we can find a use for our discarded writing after all). The directors of Headspace “focus on atmosphere first and foremost” and hire poets to write us to our dreams by “conjuring images and feelings.” They work to vary structures in each story because they want “to keep people’s brains from scanning for a familiar pattern.” Stories on the Calm app slow as they progress, and they “intentionally get less interesting.” If you do all of these things, you can make your storytelling become ambient sound—as useful and unremarkable as white noise.

Sleep stories save us from ourselves. The director of the Yale Center for Sleep Medicine explains that “a bedtime story works by detracting the mind from self-sabotaging thoughts and worries, which allows the body’s adrenaline to come down so the brain can transition into the sleep state.” Another expert isolates sensory description as an important quality that allows us to imagine another place and escape the anxious mind. The pacing of the sentences—and their quiet and slow and steady delivery—is crucial because, as the voice of Get Sleepy says, it “taps into the brain’s innate rhythmicity.” In the early stages of sleep, the brain experiences “this more stable, less variable rhythmic pattern of activity” that we hear in the sentences of sleep stories. And, of course, the plots are boring, and by boring us, sleep-writers slow the release of norepinephrine. We feel sleepy; on a carpet of simple words, we glide to the freedom of dreams.

The sleep stories that interest me most occur in a self-contained fictional universe, the Village of Nothing Much Happens (created by Kathryn Nicolai). Online we can even study landmarks on a map of the village: a bakery, a café, a bookshop, a library, a theater. The world of Nothing Much Happens is like the little interconnected universes of Dubliners and Winesburg, Ohio, except the characters do not suffer and the epiphanies are meant to release us from our own frantic search for meaning. The village is where the narrator on the sleeper car presumably lives and where she will return.

In the introduction to a book of selected sleep stories, Nicolai recommends putting away all screens before we go to bed. She identifies modern technologies as a cause of our sleeplessness, and she sets her stories in an idyllic tech-less world. Here, in the Village of Nothing Much Happens, all the books are paperbacks and none of them disappoint. The stoves are powered by gas; the kettles are not electric. Music plays from record players, music boxes, and radios. We find handwritten letters, a recipe on an index card, postcards, albums of old photos, a ticket stub from a play, a note slipped by a stranger into a coat pocket. The characters handle paper notebooks, planners, newspapers, magazines, and calendars. On a snowy day, the kids don’t sit indoors scrolling through TikTok; they gather outside, throw snowballs, and sled down hills. A narrator hangs a clothesline in the backyard of a cottage; she spots a hot air balloon; she marvels at the night sky drained of light pollution, twinkling with stars. We are all addicted and tormented by our devices, and these dream stories are our fantasies, sketches of a little perfect worlds where there are no smartphones pinging us away from our tangible lives. Where there is no one to bother us.

Nicolai’s narrators often arrive at little realizations around life and our existence in this universe, as her storytelling urges us to sleep but also to wake the next day a little more attentive. In the grocery store, the narrator finds herself “suddenly so grateful that these cookies had made their way from up there to down here, onto the shelf of my neighborhood store.” In another story, the narrator muses how “adults tried to tell me magic wasn’t real, that it was only something that happened in stories, but to me there were so many signs of it everywhere that it seemed like the adults were only trying to convince themselves.” Elsewhere the narrator takes us along for “that flash of understanding that sometimes happens when we step outside our own perspectives: that every person is the main character of their own story and we move in and out of the frame of others’ stories as supporting characters or background players but we never really know any story but our own.”

This final realization moves from cliché to something real: the limits of ourselves. It’s a terrifying thought—or a beautiful one, if you accept the reality of our difference and transience on this earth. Another writer would have taken the next leap, would have moved into another epiphany, a string of lyricism or sullen contemplation on our human condition. But we find ourselves in a sleep story; the goal is to fall asleep. Nicolai writes on with no theatricality or ego, like a tennis player who eschews winners for the pleasure of a long and pointless rally.

It would be easy to critique the limits of the characters’ observations, the prose’s lack of texture, the vagaries of place and time. But sleep-writing fulfills its purpose. In another story, a rare meta-commentary, the narrator describes her love of words. “Adoxography,” she says, “is pretty writing about simple stuff.” While “quiescent”means “quiet and not active, and it’s good for everyone and everything sometimes.” Elsewhere, Nicolai explains another reason for the simplicity and restraint of her characters, images, and realizations. “As a little girl watching old Christmas movies from the couch,” she writes, “I’d expected my grown-up holidays to be full of train trips through snowy countrysides and nights out in swanky cocktail clubs.” But now, “as an actual adult, my holidays have been infinitely simpler,” “a time to do some favorite things, to be closer to the people I called family, to wonder at the beauty of fresh snow or a lighted Christmas tree through a stranger’s window.” The lesson is clear: as we mature, we should discover joy in the details of life. Not countrysides, not train trips, not cocktail clubs, but the familiar: snow and the lights on a Christmas tree.
There is something comforting but also heartbreaking about all of this. Why, when I listen to these stories of small observations and peace, do I feel loss?

Following the 2016 election, “Trump-induced insomnia” began to spread across America, and sleep podcasts began to proliferate. The need for sleep stories spiked in 2020, when the pandemic killed millions worldwide and suspended our way of life. Insomnia increased globally, classified by experts as a special kind of sleeplessness, “coronasomnia.” We still have other catastrophes to worry about: the climate crisis; increasing political violence; the erosion of women’s rights; mass deportations; inflation; and the ever-present feeling, as Olga Tokarczuk described in her Nobel lecture, “that there is something wrong with the world.”

In Sleepless, a recent exploration of insomnia, Marie Darrieussecq surveys the genre of insomnia writing before hypothesizing that “these days,” insomnia emerges from a new cause, now that “we are summoned by planetary time; it travels through us.” Insomnia, she ponders, may be seeping into us from outside us, asking: “Hidden in our attics, crouching beneath our mattresses, sliding between the joists of time, where does insomnia come from? From ghosts? From the brain? From a troubled soul? From the world?” As she searches for cures for her own insomnia, Darrieussecq advances an argument that we suffer a collective insomnia. We pass through a waking sleep as we pillage resources to further our consumption; we accept the evils of inequality and climate change; we patter through a societal nightmare, not flinching at environmental abuses, wide awake.

It’s said the pandemic accelerated the societal changes already underway; the fissures ruptured and we fell into the future. The coronavirus focused its killing on the elderly, but its psychological damage targeted millennials and Gen Z. Everything we grew up with has changed. We have been experimented on by the milk companies, Big Pharma and Big Cereal, and the rich boys at social media companies who drowned us in blue light, cast us into extreme psycho-digital pandemonium. We contend with the attention economy, and we struggle with the demands of breaking news, unprecedented times, and little entertainments, short videos, doom scrolls, red hearts. A century from now our time will be documented as one of unpredictable and extreme instability and change. When you try to make it across a dark room, you reach out your hand, feeling for a stable table or chair. Now, in the 2010s and 2020s, millions of grown-ups reach for the stability of bedtime stories, those furniture pieces in the rooms of our childhoods.

While the sleep genre speaks to individual people, its stories avoid the individual. They avoid idiosyncratic details or even sketches of characters. In Nothing Much Happens, the narrator is often alone, and when strangers step into the frame, they add to her peace; when romantic partners appear, the I becomes a frictionless we. Sleep story writers avoid defining their characters as they populate their dream-worlds with vague images: books, blankets, coffee shops, trees. This way it takes less effort to imagine, and there is no risk of difference. Sleep stories provide an escape from the self—and at the ends of hectic days, as the author of Dopamine Nation explained, “our culture is demanding that we focus on ourselves so much that what it’s creating is this deep need to escape ourselves.”

Adam Zagajewski once spoke about the rejection of poetry and contemplation by contemporary society and how now “a moment of reflection is hazardous to health; you have to run, you have to escape from yourself.” I used to be ruthless on this topic. Life should be a confrontation with the self, I argued in the haughty idealism of my early 20s, and we must set aside our devices, our superhero movies and reality shows, our celebrity gossip and Instagram feeds, to instead think on our human condition, to deepen our inner lives, and to make space in our hearts for the necessity of solitude and travail.

Since then I have been baptized in the disappointments of adulthood—in the millennial economy, in heartbreak, in the loss of friends, in the pandemic, in political catastrophe, in the collapse of institutions, in the erasure of human rights, and in an appalling lack of action on climate change, which threatens the obliteration of all species, including our own. For these reasons I have changed. The world batters our optimism and dreams; maybe it is okay to seek comfort rather than contemplate our own mortality without end. Maybe it is okay to escape in the solace of a story that doesn’t matter and where the ending is always a good one, because there is no ending and because you are falling asleep, because you are falling asleep without even knowing it, because you are asleep now, and no one can haunt you or hurt you, and your fretful mind—at least for an extended moment, for a brief interval of darkness—can finally rest.
